title: No-Thought as the Principle
author: Zhanran
excerpt: The Avataṃsaka Sutra, chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata, says: “There is not a single being who does not possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata; it is only because of deluded thoughts and inverted attachments that they fail to realize it. inline.s: The Wondrous Gate of Practice
The Practice of the Three No’s
Cultivating the Practice of No-Thought
The Avataṃsaka Sutra,
chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata, says:
“There is not a single being who does not possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata; it is only because of deluded thoughts and inverted attachments that they fail to realize it;
if they are free of deluded thoughts
, the all-knowing wisdom, the natural wisdom, and the unobstructed wisdom will manifest before them.”

(Translation: Every being possesses the wisdom of the Tathāgata, but because of deluded thoughts and inverted attachment, they cannot realize it; if they are free of deluded thoughts, the all-knowing wisdom, the natural wisdom, and the unobstructed wisdom will manifest before them.)

[Inverted attachment] To identify with deluded thoughts, believing the things one thinks of are real (inversion), and thus to be constrained into thinking, feeling, and acting in a certain way (attachment).
Master Guifeng said:

“All phenomena are like dreams, as all the sages agree. Therefore deluded thoughts are originally quiescent, and sense-objects are originally empty. The empty, quiescent mind is a spiritual awareness that is never dimmed.
This empty, quiescent awareness is your true nature

Whether deluded or awakened, the mind is originally self-aware; it does not arise dependent on conditions, nor does it arise because of objects. The single word ‘awareness’ is the gate of all wonders.”

[Empty, quiescent awareness] The empty, quiescent awareness is the awareness of no-thought; to distinguish it from the object-grasping awareness of seeing, hearing, and knowing, it is also called “spiritual awareness.” (See
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Womb of the Tathāgata
.) The Śūraṅgama Sutra says:

“To establish awareness upon knowing and seeing is the root of ignorance; to have knowing and seeing without seeing is nirvāṇa, flawless and truly pure.” Master Hanshan’s Notes on the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra says: “When the mind is quiescent and aware, apart from both truth and falsehood, this is called self-realized sublime wisdom.”
[The single word ‘awareness’ is the gate of all wonders] This ‘awareness’ of the empty, quiescent awareness is the gate of all wonders.

“Because from beginningless time they have been deluded, they wrongly grasp body and mind as the self and give rise to thoughts of greed, hatred, and the rest. If they meet a good friend who opens up the truth, they suddenly awaken to the empty, quiescent awareness. Since awareness has no thought and no form, where is the mark of a self or of a person?

Awakening to the emptiness of all marks, the mind is naturally without thought; when a thought arises, immediately awaken to it, and the awakening itself dissolves it. The wondrous gate of practice lies in this alone.”

[Awakening to the emptiness of all marks, the mind is naturally without thought; when a thought arises, immediately awaken to it, and the awakening dissolves it. The wondrous gate of practice lies here] To awaken to the illusoriness of all marks, the mind naturally gives rise to no thought; if a deluded thought arises, one must immediately awaken to the fact that one is mistaking illusion for reality and being turned by it; the moment one awakens to this, the deluded thought dies away. The wondrous gate of practice is right here!
“Therefore, although one may cultivate all the myriad practices,
one takes no-thought alone as the principle
. If one attains the knowing and seeing of no-thought
(that is, attains the knowing and seeing that are free of thought)

, then love and hatred naturally grow mild, compassion and wisdom naturally brighten, karmic offenses naturally cease, and merit and practice naturally advance. Having understood that all marks are not marks, one naturally has the practice of no-practice. When afflictions are exhausted, birth and death come to an end. When arising and ceasing cease, quiescent illumination appears, and its function is inexhaustible — this is called Buddhahood.”

[Attain the knowing and seeing of no-thought] To attain the knowing and seeing that are free of thought — that is, to know without giving rise to thought and to see without giving rise to thought, like a mirror reflecting objects, without “establishing awareness upon knowing and seeing.” [Establish awareness upon knowing and seeing] The Śūraṅgama Sutra says:
“To establish awareness upon knowing and seeing is the root of ignorance; to have knowing and seeing without seeing is nirvāṇa, flawless and truly pure.”
(the Chan school)
was transmitted through six generations in this way. By the time of Heze
(Master Shenhui of Heze Monastery in Luoyang in the Tang dynasty, a foremost disciple of the Sixth Patriarch)

, other schools were contending on every side; those who sought silent accord found no favorable occasion. Reflecting again on Bodhidharma’s prediction of the dangling thread, and fearing that the essential doctrine would be cut off, he therefore proclaimed plainly: the single word ‘awareness’ is the gate of all wonders
(this awareness of the empty, quiescent awareness is the gate of all wonders)
(Preface to the Collected Essentials of the Chan Sources)

[Bodhidharma’s prediction of the dangling thread] Master Guifeng’s Great Commentary on the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “According to Bodhidharma’s prediction, after six generations the life of the teaching would hang by a thread.” This means that the transmission of the Chan school after the Sixth Patriarch was in danger as precarious as a thousand pounds hanging by a single thread. In fact, after the Sixth Patriarch, the Northern school, led by Shenxiu — “Dharma-master of the two capitals and teacher of three emperors” — and his disciple Puji, replaced the heart of Chan, the sudden teaching, with the doctrine of gradual awakening. Had not Master Shenhui staked his life on the matter, the “Battle of Huatai” restoring the essential doctrine, how could there have been the later golden age in which the true transmission of Chan spread throughout the world? [The Battle of Huatai] In the twentieth year of Kaiyuan (732), Master Shenhui, risking his life, convened at Huatai (present-day Hua County, Henan) the “Assembly of Huatai,” open to all comers, and publicly debated with the renowned monk Chongyuan — “famed in the two capitals and known across the seas” — criticizing the Northern school of Shenxiu for “a line of succession that is collateral and a Dharma gate that is gradual,” and re-establishing the sudden teaching of the Sixth Patriarch.

[Dharma-master of the two capitals and teacher of three emperors] The “two capitals” are Chang’an in the west and Luoyang in the east; the “three emperors” are Empress Wu Zetian, Emperor Zhongzong, and Emperor Ruizong of Tang. [Sudden teaching] The teaching that “points directly to the source, without passing through the stages, seeing the nature and attaining Buddhahood.” Its principle is: suddenly awaken to the self-nature, which is originally pure, originally complete, and whose very nature is Buddha. [Without passing through the stages] Ordinarily a bodhisattva, from ordinary being to Buddhahood, must pass through fifty-two stages: the ten stages of faith, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transferences, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment, spanning three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas. The Chan school’s pace of practice is far, far swifter, and does not pass through these stages one by one. [Asaṃkhyeya kalpa] Translated into Chinese as “an incalculable number of kalpas.” [See the nature and attain Buddhahood] See one’s original nature, then cultivate according to that nature, perfectly accomplishing the Buddha path.
Question: What is right mindfulness?

Answer: The principle of the Pure Land school is to recite the Buddha’s name and seek birth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Therefore, for the Pure Land school, the thought of reciting the Buddha’s name is right mindfulness, and all other thoughts are deluded thoughts. For example, the “right mindfulness” in “right mindfulness at life’s end,” “birth through right mindfulness,” and “summon up right mindfulness” all refer to the thought of reciting the Buddha’s name. The principle of the Chan school, however, is to illumine the mind and see the nature, reaching straight to unsurpassed bodhi. So, for the Chan school, right mindfulness is the empty, quiescent awareness — that is, the awareness of no-thought. Master Yongming said:
“Right mindfulness is knowing without thought; for if there were no knowing at all, how could it be right mindfulness?”
(from the Zongjing Lu) Hence an ancient worthy said:
“All thoughts are delusion.”
Excerpted from
An In-Depth Explanation of the Platform Sutra

The three no’s — no-thought, no-form, and no-abiding — are the core practice of the Platform Sutra. No-thought: amid thought, no thought; no-form: amid form, detachment from form; no-abiding: amid objects, no pondering. Achieve not being turned by thoughts within, and not being drawn by objects without. No-thought is great samādhi, no-form is great discipline, and no-abiding is great wisdom.

[The Master addressed the assembly: Good friends! The true teaching originally has no sudden or gradual, but people’s natures are naturally sharp or dull. The deluded cultivate gradually, while the awakened awaken suddenly. Once you know your own mind and see your own nature, there is no difference between them. Hence the provisional names of sudden and gradual.]
The Sixth Patriarch

addressed the assembly: Good friends! The true teaching originally has no sudden or gradual, but people’s faculties are naturally sharp or dull. The deluded enter by gradual cultivation, while the awakened enter by sudden realization. As long as you know your own mind and see your own nature, there is no difference between them. Hence the provisional names of sudden awakening and gradual cultivation.
[Provisional name] A false name. All phenomena have no real essence and originally have no names; people give them provisional names. The Lotus Sutra,
chapter two on Expedient Means, says: “Only through provisional names to guide sentient beings.”

[Good friends! In this Dharma gate of mine, from the beginning, no-thought is established as the principle, no-form as the essence, and no-abiding as the basis. “No-form” means to be amid form and yet detached from form. “No-thought” means to be amid thought and yet without thought. “No-abiding” is the original nature of human beings: amid the good and evil, the fair and foul of the world, even amid enmity and kinship, when words are sharp and spoken in provocation or deceit and contention, one regards them all as empty and does not ponder recompense or retaliation; within each thought, one does not ponder the objects before one. If past thought, present thought, and future thought continue in unbroken succession, this is called bondage; if one’s thoughts do not abide in any phenomenon, one is without bondage. This is taking no-abiding as the basis.

Good friends! In this sudden-teaching Dharma gate of mine, handed down from the Patriarch Bodhidharma, no-thought is first established as the principle, no-form as the essence, and no-abiding as the basis. “No-form” means to be amid form and detached from form, not turned by form. “No-thought” means to be amid thought and yet without thought, not giving rise to a mind upon thoughts, not drawn by thoughts. “No-abiding” is the original nature of human beings: amid the good and evil, the fair and foul of the world, even amid enmity and kinship, when words are sharp and spoken in provocation, deceit, and contention, one knows that all these are illusory (regarding them all as empty), and does not ponder recompense or retaliation; within each thought one does not ponder the objects before one (amid objects, no pondering). If past, present, and future thoughts continue in unbroken succession, thought giving rise to thought, this is called bondage; but if amid all phenomena one’s thoughts never abide in objects and give rise to a mind, with no defilement and no clinging, one is without bondage and attains freedom. This is taking no-abiding (amid objects, no pondering) as the basis.

[No-form] Not clinging to form; amid form, detached from form. [Amid thought, no thought] Do not suppress thoughts so they cannot arise; rather, when a thought arises, know it and do not follow it. Suppressing thoughts not only tenses the whole body, but the moment one stops suppressing, the deluded thoughts become even more active. [No-abiding is
the original nature of human beings

] The original nature of human beings is non-abiding: knowing all phenomena are empty, one neither clings nor defiles; whereas the habitual disposition of human beings is abiding: wrongly grasping all phenomena as real, one clings and defiles. [Not pondering the objects before one] Not pondering the objects presently before one (amid objects, no pondering): seeing is only seeing, hearing is only hearing — with a mind at ease, free of attachment.
The Diamond Sutra says:
“One should not give rise to a mind dwelling on form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling on sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects; one should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.”
The phrase “give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere”

means to act with a straightforward mind, uninfluenced by the conditions of objects (temptation, hardship, or coercion). Therefore one should work on the thought of the present moment — this is the wondrous method of governing the mind right at the point of contact with objects.
[Good friends! To be outwardly detached from all marks is called no-form. To be able to detach from marks is to have the Dharma-body pure. This is taking no-form as the essence.]

Good friends! To be outwardly detached from all marks, not turned by them, is called no-form; to be able to detach from marks is to have the Dharma-body of the self-nature pure. This is taking no-form as the essence.

[Good friends! To have the mind undefiled amid all objects is called no-thought. On one’s own thoughts, always detach from all objects, and do not give rise to a mind upon objects. If one merely thinks of nothing at all and eliminates all thought, the moment thought is cut off one dies and is reborn elsewhere — this is a great error. Let students of the Way ponder this! If one does not understand the true meaning of the Dharma, to err oneself may be pardonable, but to go on to exhort others, one’s own delusion being unseen, is also to slander the Buddhist sutras. Therefore no-thought is established as the principle.]

Good friends! To have the mind undefiled amid all conditions and objects is called no-thought. No-thought means: on one’s own thoughts, always detach from all objects (“give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere”), and do not give rise to a mind upon objects (“do not give rise to a mind dwelling on form, nor on sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects”). If one supposes that no-thought is merely “thinking of nothing at all and eliminating all thought,” this is a great error! For the moment thought is cut off, one dies and is reborn elsewhere, still revolving in saṃsāra. Let students of the Way ponder this deeply! If one does not recognize the true meaning of the true Dharma, to err oneself may be pardonable, but if one uses such a mistaken method to exhort others, then, besides one’s own delusion and failure to see the Way, one incurs the offense of slandering the Buddhist sutras — with consequences of the utmost severity. Therefore no-thought is established as the principle.

To always detach from all objects on one’s own thoughts, and not give rise to a mind upon objects” — this is precisely: “Do not give rise to a mind dwelling on form, nor on sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects; give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.” Merely detach from objects on one’s own thoughts, and do not let a mind arise upon phenomena.

Question: The Sixth Patriarch says: “If one merely thinks of nothing at all and eliminates all thought, the moment thought is cut off one dies and is reborn elsewhere — this is a great error.” Yet the Fourth Patriarch, Master Daoxin, says: “The great Way is vast and open; cut off thinking and cut off deliberation.” These two statements seem opposed; which should one follow?

Answer: The Sixth Patriarch was addressing the mistaken practice of his time, which took “thinking of nothing at all and eliminating all thought” as the ultimate. Later in this sutra, he criticizes the Chan master Wolun’s “able to cut off all thinking,” also because Wolun took “able to cut off all thinking” as the ultimate. Their error lies in taking “eliminating all thought” and “able to cut off all thinking” as the ultimate — those who know only the great death and not the great life.

Chan master Dahui said: “This old fellow has always loved what the Venerable Zhenjing said: nowadays people mostly attain a body and mind that are still and extinct, the before and after cut off, resting and ceasing, one thought enduring ten thousand years, like an incense burner in an old temple, cold and desolate — and they take this as the ultimate. Little do they know that they are being obstructed and blinded by this wondrous state, so that their own true knowing and seeing cannot appear, and their spiritual powers and radiance cannot shine forth.” (Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dahui Pujue)
In fact, in cultivation there are two great stages: preservation (bao) and allowance (ren). The Fourth Patriarch, Daoxin, gives a detailed teaching on this.

The Fourth Patriarch said to Farong: “The hundred thousand Dharma gates all return to the square inch of the mind; the wondrous virtues countless as the Ganges’ sands all lie in the source of the mind. All the gates of discipline, concentration, and wisdom, and all spiritual powers and transformations, are complete within you, never apart from your mind. All afflictions and karmic hindrances are originally empty and quiescent. All causes and effects are like dreams and illusions. There is no triple world to leave, no bodhi to seek. Human and non-human are equal in nature and mark. The great Way is vast and open; cut off thinking and cut off deliberation. Such a Dharma you have already attained, lacking nothing — how does it differ from Buddha? (Note: ‘Such a Dharma you have already attained’ means Farong’s work of preservation — cutting off thinking and deliberation — had already been accomplished, so what follows instructs him in the work of allowance — letting the mind be at ease.) There is no other Dharma; you need only let the mind be at ease, do not practice contemplation, do not still the mind, do not give rise to greed or anger, do not harbor sorrow or anxiety, and, at ease and unobstructed, freely and boundlessly, do not contrive good, do not contrive evil — in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, whatever meets the eye, whatever condition arises, all is the wondrous function of the Buddha. Joyous and without worry, this is called Buddha.” Farong said: “If I am not permitted to practice contemplation, then when objects arise, how should the mind deal with them?” The master said: “Objects and conditions have no good or evil; good and evil arise from the mind. If the mind does not forcibly name them, how can deluded feelings arise? When deluded feelings do not arise, the true mind functions in knowing everywhere. You need only follow the mind at ease, with nothing further to remedy — this is called the eternally abiding Dharma-body.” (For detailed commentary, see
The Fourth Patriarch’s Teaching to Farong

The Diamond Sutra says: “Do not give rise to a mind dwelling on form, nor on sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects; give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.” The work of preservation is “not giving rise to a mind dwelling on form, nor on sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects.” The work of allowance is “giving rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.”

[Good friends! Why establish no-thought as the principle? Only because there are people who speak of seeing the nature but, being deluded, give rise to thoughts upon objects, and upon these thoughts give rise to wrong views; from this arise all the defilements and delusions. The self-nature originally has not a single dharma to attain; if there is anything to attain, to speak falsely of fortune and misfortune is itself defilement and wrong view. Therefore this Dharma gate establishes no-thought as the principle.]

Good friends! Why establish no-thought as the principle? Because deluded people who merely speak of seeing the nature give rise to thoughts upon objects, and upon these thoughts give rise to wrong views; from this arise all defilements and delusions. But the self-nature originally has not a single dharma to attain; if there is anything to attain, to speak falsely of fortune and misfortune is worldly wrong view. Therefore this Dharma gate establishes no-thought as the principle.

All phenomena are illusory, so the self-nature attains not a single dharma; why then give rise to thoughts upon objects? This is precisely where beings are deluded. One should regard everything from the standpoint of the true mark of all phenomena — this is the Way.

Worldly people have their minds bound up in fortune and misfortune, gain and loss. If they can understand that these are all illusions, with nothing to be attained, the mind empties, free of obstruction, and only then can they enter the Way.

[Good friends! “No” — what is negated? “Thought” — what is thought of? “No” negates the marks of duality and the mind of all defilements; “thought” is thought of the true-suchness of the original nature. True-suchness is the essence of thought, and thought is the function of true-suchness. It is the true-suchness of the self-nature that gives rise to thought; it is not the eyes, ears, nose, or tongue that can think. Because true-suchness has a nature, it gives rise to thought. If there were no true-suchness, the eyes and ears, forms and sounds would immediately perish.]

Good friends! The “no” of no-thought — what does it negate? The “thought” of no-thought — what does it think of? The “no” of no-thought negates all marks of distinction such as right and wrong, good and evil, fair and foul, and the mind of all manner of afflictions; the “thought” of no-thought thinks of the true-suchness of the original nature. True-suchness is the essence of thought, and thought is the function of true-suchness. It is the true-suchness of the self-nature that gives rise to thought, not the eyes, ears, nose, or tongue. Because the true-suchness of the self-nature functions, it is able to think; if the true-suchness of the self-nature did not function, the eye could not see forms, and the ear could not hear sounds.

[Good friends! When the true-suchness of the self-nature gives rise to thought, although the six faculties have seeing, hearing, awareness, and knowing, they are not defiled by the myriad objects, and the true nature is ever at ease. Therefore the sutra says: Able to discern well the marks of all phenomena, yet unmoved in the ultimate truth.]

Good friends! When the true-suchness of the self-nature gives rise to thought, although the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) have seeing, hearing, awareness, and knowing, they are not defiled by the myriad objects, and the true nature is ever at ease (unaffected and undefiled). Therefore the Vimalakīrti Sutra,

chapter one on the Buddha Land, says: “Able to discern well the marks of all phenomena, yet unmoved in the ultimate truth.” (Able to perceive all phenomena clearly, while the mind is not moved by these illusions.)

[Ultimate truth] The supreme truth, that is, the true mark of all phenomena. The Buddha said: “All phenomena are false; that point at which they cease is called reality, is called the true mark, is called the Dharma realm, is called ultimate wisdom, is called the truth of the ultimate meaning, is called the emptiness of the ultimate meaning.” (The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra, fascicle forty, the chapter on Kauṇḍinya)

When the true-suchness of the self-nature gives rise to thought, although the six faculties have seeing, hearing, awareness, and knowing, they are not defiled by the myriad objects, and the true nature is ever at ease. — This is “giving rise to a mind that dwells nowhere,” this is “giving rise to a mind that abides nowhere.” If, upon facing objects, one ponders them and is carried away by them, one is scattered, deluded, and ill at ease.

Able to discern well the marks of all phenomena, yet unmoved in the ultimate truth.” — The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “It is like the light of the eye perceiving clearly the objects before it, its radiance complete, free of love and hate.”
Master Hanshan said:
(Beings)
have all along taken the arising-and-ceasing mind of deluded thoughts as true, and so amid the conditions of the six sense-objects they take all manner of illusions as real.”
(from the Mengyou Ji,
Letter in Reply to Vice-Censor Zheng Kunyan). In the Śūraṅgama Sutra, the Buddha says:
All beings, from beginningless time, undergo birth and death in succession, all because they do not know the permanent true mind, the nature that is pure and luminous in essence
(all because they do not know how to abide in the true mind, this nature that is pure and luminous in essence)
, and employ deluded thoughts
(and instead employ deluded thoughts)
; these thoughts being unreal, there is transmigration.”

[True mind, the nature pure and luminous in essence] The nature pure and luminous in essence is the luminous and wondrous essence that is pure by nature. Grammatically, “the nature pure and luminous in essence” is an appositive modifying the noun “true mind.” [Transmigration] Birth and death in discrete segments and birth and death through transformation. [Birth and death in discrete segments] Beings in the three realms and six paths, due to the ripening of good and evil karma, have lives of definite length and bodies of distinct forms, hence their birth and death is called “birth and death in discrete segments.” Those who end birth and death in discrete segments escape saṃsāra. [Birth and death through transformation] Sages of the three vehicles, having cut off delusions of views and thought and ended birth and death in discrete segments, in the course of their practice see delusion gradually extinguished and realization gradually increased; this migration between delusion and awakening differs at each stage, and the passage from an earlier stage to a later stage is like a single birth and death, its transformations wondrous, unfathomable, and inconceivable, hence it is called “birth and death through transformation.” Those who end birth and death through transformation perfectly realize Buddhahood.

[Good friends! With wisdom’s contemplation, illumine within and without, and know your own original mind. If you know your original mind, this is original liberation. If you attain liberation, this is the prajñā samādhi, this is “no-thought.”]

Good friends! With wisdom’s contemplation, illumine within and without, and know your own original mind. If you know your original mind, you attain original liberation. If you attain original liberation, this is the prajñā samādhi, this is no-thought.
[Know your own original mind] To realize the original state of the mind — luminous, clear, still, and quiescent. The Mahāyāna Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground says:
“If one can contemplate that the mind and its nature are empty, delusion and hindrances will not arise, and one attains liberation.”
[Original liberation] When the mind is empty, objects are naturally empty; all phenomena having no bondage, one is liberated from the very beginning.

[What is called no-thought? If, seeing all phenomena, the mind is undefiled and unattached, this is no-thought. Its function extends everywhere, yet it clings nowhere. Merely purify the original mind, so that the six consciousnesses go out the six gates and, amid the six sense-objects, remain undefiled and unmixed, coming and going freely, functioning everywhere without obstruction — this is the prajñā samādhi, freedom and liberation, called the practice of no-thought. If one thinks of nothing at all and forces thought to cease, this is bondage to phenomena and is called a one-sided view.]

What is meant by “no-thought”? If, seeing all things (all phenomena), the mind is undefiled and unattached (without discriminating calculations, deluded clinging, or love and hate), this is no-thought. The mind, in its function, extends everywhere, yet clings nowhere. Merely purify the original mind, so that the six consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind consciousness) go out through the six gates (that is, the six faculties: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) and, amid the six sense-objects
(form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects)

, neither intermix greed, hatred, and ignorance nor be defiled by them, coming and going freely, functioning everywhere without obstruction — this is the prajñā samādhi, freedom and liberation, called the “practice of no-thought.” If one thinks of nothing at all and forces thoughts not to arise, this is bondage to phenomena and is called a one-sided view.

Therefore, “no-thought” does not mean having no thoughts at all; rather, it means: seeing all phenomena, the mind is undefiled and unattached, without deluded clinging or love and hate. That is, as the Diamond Sutra says:
“Do not give rise to a mind dwelling on form, nor on sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects; give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.”
That is to say: merely detach from objects on one’s own thoughts, and do not let a mind arise upon phenomena.

[Force thought to cease] Not permitting thought to arise. [Bondage to phenomena] Clinging one-sidedly to the Dharma, quoting out of context, not knowing how to apply it flexibly, and thus being bound instead of liberated. [One-sided view] A pernicious view that inclines to one extreme (rushing to the other extreme).
This sutra says:
“If one thinks of nothing at all and forces thought to cease, this is bondage to phenomena and is called a one-sided view.”

Therefore correct practice is not to think of nothing at all, but to enter awakening at the very point of seeing, hearing, awareness, and knowing. The “seeing, hearing, awareness, and knowing” that arise when the six faculties contact the six objects, although the root of delusion, are also the essential gate of awakening and entering the Way. The difference between “delusion” and “awakening” lies solely in whether one can, at the point of seeing, hearing, awareness, and knowing, turn delusion into awakening and turn consciousness into wisdom. As the later text says:
“When the true-suchness of the self-nature gives rise to thought, although the six faculties have seeing, hearing, awareness, and knowing, they are not defiled by the myriad objects.”
[Awakening] Seeing all phenomena, the mind is undefiled and unattached (without discriminating calculations, deluded clinging, or love and hate).

[Good friends! One who awakens to the Dharma of no-thought penetrates all phenomena; one who awakens to the Dharma of no-thought sees the realm of all Buddhas; one who awakens to the Dharma of no-thought reaches the stage of Buddhahood.]

Good friends! One who awakens to the Dharma of no-thought penetrates all Buddha-dharmas; one who awakens to the Dharma of no-thought sees the realm of all Buddhas; one who awakens to the Dharma of no-thought reaches the stage of Buddhahood.
